name: Plasmablastic lymphoma
aliases: plasmablastic lymphoma of the oral cavity

clinicalPearls: Classically presents as a rapidly growing mass in the oral cavity or jaw of an HIV-positive patient, but can arise at many extranodal sites including the gastrointestinal tract
Strongly linked to immunodeficiency (HIV infection, transplantation, older age) and frequently associated with Epstein-Barr virus
Tumour cells resemble plasmablasts or immunoblasts with a very high proliferation index

The immunophenotype straddles B-cell and plasma-cell differentiation: pan-B-cell markers such as CD20 and PAX5 are usually negative or weak while plasma-cell markers CD138, CD38, and MUM1/IRF4 are positive
MYC rearrangement is common and is associated with a more aggressive course
Overlap with plasmablastic plasma-cell myeloma requires correlation with clinical features, imaging, and any paraprotein
In situ hybridisation for EBV-encoded RNA is positive in many cases, especially those linked to immunodeficiency
reference.pathophysiology: Plasmablastic lymphoma is an aggressive large B-cell neoplasm whose cells have differentiated to the plasmablast stage, losing mature B-cell antigens while acquiring a plasma-cell secretory phenotype. It arises predominantly in immunodeficient hosts, in whom impaired immune surveillance permits Epstein-Barr virus-driven proliferation of terminally differentiating B-cells. Frequent rearrangement of the MYC oncogene amplifies proliferative drive, producing the characteristic high growth fraction and rapidly enlarging masses. Because the neoplastic cells resemble plasma cells, the tumour lies at the interface between lymphoma and plasma-cell neoplasia.
additionalDifferentials: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma with plasmablastic features
additionalInvestigations: Biopsy with immunohistochemistry showing CD138/CD38/MUM1 positivity and loss of CD20/PAX5
In situ hybridisation for EBV-encoded RNA
HIV testing and assessment of immune status
Serum and urine protein electrophoresis to help distinguish from plasma-cell myeloma
PET-CT and bone marrow examination for staging
redFlags: Rapidly enlarging oral or facial mass causing airway or feeding compromise
Gastrointestinal bleeding or obstruction from mucosal disease
Bulky disease with tumour lysis risk given the high proliferation rate
Concurrent opportunistic infection in the immunocompromised host
reference.prognosis: The disease is aggressive with generally short survival, though control of HIV with antiretroviral therapy and intensive combination chemotherapy can improve outcomes; MYC rearrangement and advanced stage predict worse results.
pitfalls: Excluding lymphoma because CD20 is negative, when plasma-cell markers confirm the diagnosis
Confusing plasmablastic lymphoma with plasma-cell myeloma without integrating clinical and serological data
Overlooking underlying HIV infection at presentation
Failing to test for EBV and MYC, which inform diagnosis and prognosis
references: Swerdlow SH et al. WHO monograph on lymphoid neoplasms
management: Confirm HIV status with baseline CD4 count and viral load, as this drives prognosis and treatment intensity
Stage with PET-CT and consider cerebrospinal fluid examination given the aggressive, extranodal-prone biology
Distinguish from plasma-cell myeloma by correlating morphology and immunophenotype before choosing therapy
Surgery has no curative role; treat primarily with systemic therapy, as biopsy is diagnostic only
Favor an intensified anthracycline-based, continuous-infusion regimen such as a dose-adjusted EPOCH-type approach over standard R-CHOP-type therapy, given the very high proliferation index
Add rituximab only if the tumor is CD20-positive, since many plasmablastic lymphomas are CD20-negative
Continue antiretroviral therapy through chemotherapy if tolerated
Provide prophylaxis against Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia, herpes zoster, and Candida during treatment
Assess and mitigate tumor lysis risk before and during the first cycle given the high proliferative rate and bulky disease
Individualize involved-site radiotherapy for palliation of a localized, symptomatic, or bulky mass
Consider standard salvage chemotherapy followed by consolidative autologous stem cell transplantation for relapsed or refractory disease in appropriate candidates
Assess treatment response with PET-CT using the Deauville scale, timed appropriately after chemotherapy or radiotherapy to avoid false-positive uptake
Continue serial CD4 count and HIV viral load monitoring alongside oncologic follow-up in HIV-associated cases

Refer promptly to hematology-oncology and, when HIV-associated, concurrently to infectious disease for coordinated care, with urgent referral for airway or feeding compromise or gastrointestinal bleeding or obstruction
